Hence John Apoc. IX, 9: And they had breastplates, as it were breastplates of iron. They will not be wounded.] In Hebrew לא יבצעו, for לא יפצעו. So here again Beth stands for Pe, as above in עבשר. The ancients render it very differently. But this version is most fitting ^{(4)}.

[III, 314] 5. They will march through the city.] In Hebrew בעיר ישקו, a verb derived from the noun שוק, that is, leg; as in Es. XXXIII, 4: כמשק גבים שוקק בו, as with the march of locusts he marches against it, namely the enemy against the Assyrian; that is, he marches in such a way that he cannot be turned back. For whatever you do, locusts press on, and they do not withdraw until they are sated. This coheres with what precedes, at the beginning of the same verse, which we touched on above: Your spoil is gathered as the bruchus gathers; that is, "The enemy will strip you as the bruchus strips a field, which it leaves only when it is bare." 6. Rightly, then, this enemy, however small, is terrible to men. Accordingly the Prophet had said in verse 6: Before its face the peoples will tremble; all faces will gather paleness. And in Ier. LI, 27, ילק סמר is perhaps a dreadful bruchus, as in Hesychius βρέττανα φοβερὰ [brettana phobera], a terrible locust.

Verse 10: Before it the earth is shaken, the heavens are moved; the sun and moon are darkened, [col. 479] and the stars withdraw their brightness.] Some understand earthquakes, thunder and eclipses. But Jerome holds that this is said hyperbolically: Not that the force of locusts is so great that they can move the heavens and shake the earth, but that to those suffering adversity, from the greatness of their terror, the sky seems to fall and the earth to heave. Yet the same author explains what is said at the end of the verse about the sun, moon and stars as meant literally: Because of the multitude of locusts covering the sky, the sun and moon will be turned into darkness, and the stars will withdraw their light, while the cloud of locusts set in between does not let the light reach the earth. So too Remigius on this passage: By their density and multitude they are wont to fill (read drive back) the rays of the sun from the earth, and to overshadow it like clouds. Onkelos writes that this happened in Egypt, Exod. X, 15: וחפא ית עין שמשא דארעא וחשיכת ארעא, And it (the mass of locusts) covered the eye of the sun of the land, and the land was darkened. So Pliny writes that locusts overshadow the sun. And the Historia Saracenica, p. 98, says that in the year (of the Hijra) 317 there was so great a multitude of locusts in Egypt انه منع شعاع الشمس ان تقع علي الارض [annahu manaʿa shuʿāʿ al-shams an taqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍ] that it kept the rays of the sun from reaching the earth. Likewise Eutychius, vol. 2, p. 518: ووقع بمصر من الجراد ما لا يوصف كثرته حتي منع شعاع الشمس ان تقع علي الارض [wa-waqaʿa bi-Miṣr min al-jarād mā lā yūṣafu kathratuhu ḥattā manaʿa shuʿāʿ al-shams an taqaʿa ʿalā al-arḍ] And there fell upon Egypt a countless multitude of locusts, so that it prevented the rays of the sun from reaching the earth. And Cadamosto, [III, 315] ch. 13 of the Navigations, on the deserts near the Nigritae: In the same regions we also saw a countless multitude of locusts shading the air; for they come almost every three years and darken the sky. And a little later: And they are so numerous that they shade the sky over a space of twelve miles. And Thuanus, book 84, on locusts in Syria: Flying like a dense cloud, the day being darkened at full noon, they grazed the fields all around. Hence Marcellus Palingenius in the Zodiacus, book 8:
— — — — and grim locusts veil the shining sun like a mist.

And we have shown ^{e)} that the two Hebrew names of locusts חגב and צלצל refer to this: the latter taken from shadow, the former from the veil that it spreads before the sun. Indeed, for this very reason Joel says that before them the heavens are moved, that is, the powers of the heavens, as in Matth. XXIV, 29. For since the chief power of the heaven lies in the light with which it shines upon us, why, when that light is blocked and, so to speak, extinguished, should not the power of heaven, and thus the heaven itself, be said to be moved? The earth, moreover, is said to be moved when men, the inhabitants of the earth, are shaken by grave fear or by sudden and unforeseen calamity. Examples of this expression abound everywhere in the Scriptures. If anyone objects that the Prophet's words, The sun and moon are darkened, and the stars withdraw their brightness, cannot refer to locusts, which in flight darken the sun but never the moon and stars, since they fly only by day, I shall reply with Pliny that the ancient writers reported that they do not fly by night because of the cold, not knowing that they cross even distant seas, with continuous hunger for many days.
